addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

1	# Realtime Auction Rooms
2	
3	Realtime Auction Rooms is a full-stack, server-authoritative auction platform. It enables hosts to spin up private bidding rooms, configure item catalogs, and manage live auctions, while participants join and submit concurrent bids with sub-second feedback. 
4	
5	The platform utilizes a reactive state model with Socket.IO communication, backed by MongoDB for server-authoritative concurrency and crash recovery.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Key Features
10	
11	- **Dynamic Room Management**: Instantly create and join auction rooms using secure room codes.
12	- **Server-Authoritative Concurrency**: Leverages atomic MongoDB updates (`findOneAndUpdate`) to prevent race conditions from concurrent bidders.
13	- **Synced Countdown Engine**: Server-owned auction timers are persisted as absolute deadlines, enabling mid-auction server restarts to recover and resume timers without loss of time.
14	- **Real-Time Presence Tracking**: Dynamic online/offline presence indicators for all participants.
15	- **Comprehensive Bid Logs**: Live bid histories updated in real time for all participants.
16	- **Instant Item Resolution**: Supports manual resolutions (Sell/Mark Unsold) by the host, as well as auto-sell on timer expiration.
17	- **Analytical Results Dashboard**: Displays final auction summaries, sales records, and bid logs upon auction completion.
18	
19	---
20	
21	## Tech Stack
22	
23	- **Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Socket.IO Client
24	- **Backend:** Node.js, Express 5, TypeScript, Mongoose, Socket.IO
25	- **Database:** MongoDB
26	- **Testing:** Node.js Native Test Runner
27	
28	---
29	
30	## Architecture Overview
31	
32	The system uses a decoupled client-server architecture. All state transitions are validated on the backend and broadcasted to connected clients.

35	flowchart LR
36	  Client["React Frontend"] <-->|"HTTP & WebSockets"| Server["Node.js / Express Server"]
37	  Server <-->|"Mongoose ODM"| Database[("MongoDB")]
38	```
39	
40	For a detailed walkthrough of the concurrency controls, socket lifecycles, and database schemas, see [ARCHITECTURE.md](file:///Users/arnavsingla/Desktop/Intern%20assignments/11-Auction-Assignment/Mini%20Realtime%20Auction%20Room/ARCHITECTURE.md).

114	   ```env

135	## Demo & Testing Guide
136	
137	For quick testing, you can use the built-in demo credentials on the login screen or register an anonymous alias (guest mode).
138	
139	### Testing the Concurrent Auction Lifecycle
140	
141	1. **Setup Catalog**: Log in as Host A, create a room, and add at least two items to the catalog.
142	2. **Join Bidders**: Open an Incognito Window or separate browser profile, register a bidder alias, and join using the room code generated by Host A.
143	3. **Launch Auction**: Host A clicks **Start Live Auction**. Both screens will synchronize and transition into the Live Auction Dashboard.
144	4. **Place Bids**: Submit bids from multiple tabs simultaneously. Verify that only higher bids are accepted, and lower or concurrent slower bids are rejected atomically with real-time feedback.
145	5. **Item Completion**: When the timer expires or the host resolves the item, the system automatically loads the next item in the catalog.
146	6. **Results**: Once all items are resolved, all connected clients navigate automatically to the final results screen.
147

151	
152	### Authentication Endpoints
153	
154	- `POST /api/auth/register` - Create a new user account.
155	- `POST /api/auth/login` - Authenticate and obtain JWT cookie.
156	- `POST /api/auth/logout` - Clear user authentication cookie.
157	- `GET /api/auth/me` - Get the current authenticated user context.
158	
159	### Room Endpoints
160	
161	- `POST /api/rooms` - Create a new auction room.
162	- `POST /api/rooms/:code/join` - Join an existing room with a code and alias.
163	- `GET /api/rooms/:code/summary` - Get details of an active room.
164	- `GET /api/rooms/:code/results` - Fetch final results of a completed room auction.
165	
166	### Item Endpoints
167	
168	- `POST /api/items` - Add a new item to a room's catalog.
169	- `GET /api/items/room/:roomId` - Retrieve catalog items for a room.
170	
171	---
172	
173	## Future Roadmap
174	
175	- **Team Bidding Budgets**: Group budgets and spend caps for collaborative bidding structures.
176	- **Live Chat & Reactions**: Enhance bidder engagement with interactive channels on the auction page.
177	- **Horizontal Scaling**: Transition the WebSocket layer to a Redis-backed Socket.IO adapter for multi-instance load balancing.
178	- **Bidding Pause/Resume Controls**: Empower hosts to pause and resume active countdowns.
179	- **Spectator Support**: Allow read-only viewer roles to follow live auctions without participating.

# Realtime Auction Rooms

Realtime Auction Rooms is a full-stack, server-authoritative auction platform. It enables hosts to spin up private bidding rooms, configure item catalogs, and manage live auctions, while participants join and submit concurrent bids with sub-second feedback. 

The platform utilizes a reactive state model with Socket.IO communication, backed by MongoDB for server-authoritative concurrency and crash recovery.

---

## Key Features

- **Dynamic Room Management**: Instantly create and join auction rooms using secure room codes.
- **Server-Authoritative Concurrency**: Leverages atomic MongoDB updates (`findOneAndUpdate`) to prevent race conditions from concurrent bidders.
- **Synced Countdown Engine**: Server-owned auction timers are persisted as absolute deadlines, enabling mid-auction server restarts to recover and resume timers without loss of time.
- **Real-Time Presence Tracking**: Dynamic online/offline presence indicators for all participants.
- **Comprehensive Bid Logs**: Live bid histories updated in real time for all participants.
- **Instant Item Resolution**: Supports manual resolutions (Sell/Mark Unsold) by the host, as well as auto-sell on timer expiration.
- **Analytical Results Dashboard**: Displays final auction summaries, sales records, and bid logs upon auction completion.

---

## Tech Stack

- **Frontend:** React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Socket.IO Client
- **Backend:** Node.js, Express 5, TypeScript, Mongoose, Socket.IO
- **Database:** MongoDB
- **Testing:** Node.js Native Test Runner

---

## Architecture Overview

The system uses a decoupled client-server architecture. All state transitions are validated on the backend and broadcasted to connected clients.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Client["React Frontend"] <-->|"HTTP & WebSockets"| Server["Node.js / Express Server"]
  Server <-->|"Mongoose ODM"| Database[("MongoDB")]
```

For a detailed walkthrough of the concurrency controls, socket lifecycles, and database schemas, see [ARCHITECTURE.md](file:///Users/arnavsingla/Desktop/Intern%20assignments/11-Auction-Assignment/Mini%20Realtime%20Auction%20Room/ARCHITECTURE.md).

---

## Folder Structure

```
├── backend
│   ├── src
│   │   ├── config          # Database, CORS, and Environment variables configuration
│   │   ├── controllers     # HTTP controllers handling auth, items, and rooms
│   │   ├── models          # MongoDB schemas (Bid, Item, Participant, Room, User)
│   │   ├── middleware      # Auth checks, error handling
│   │   ├── routes          # REST API endpoints
│   │   ├── services        # Core business logic (rooms, items)
│   │   ├── socket          # Socket.IO connections, handlers, and middlewares
│   │   └── utils           # Helper functions & test suites
│   └── package.json
└── frontend
    ├── src
    │   ├── app             # Router, providers, and layout setups
    │   ├── components      # Shared UI elements & Design layout
    │   ├── features        # Feature modules (Lobby, Auth, Auction, Results)
    │   ├── pages           # Router page templates
    │   ├── services        # API Client and WebSocket wrappers
    │   └── stores          # Zustand client-side state stores
    └── package.json
```

---

## Running Locally

### Prerequisites

- **Node.js** 18+
- **MongoDB** (Local instance or MongoDB Atlas Connection String)

### Step 1: Clone and Configure Backend

1. Navigate to the backend directory:
   ```bash
   cd backend
   ```
2. Install dependencies:
   ```bash
   npm install
   ```
3. Copy environment template and configure:
   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   ```
   Modify `.env` to include your MongoDB URI and set a secure `JWT_SECRET` for production:
   ```env
   PORT=3001
   MONGODB_URI=mongodb://localhost:27017/auction-room
   JWT_SECRET=<REDACTED>
   ```

### Step 2: Configure Frontend

1. Navigate to the frontend directory:
   ```bash
   cd ../frontend
   ```
2. Install dependencies:
   ```bash
   npm install
   ```
3. Copy environment template:
   ```bash
   cp .env.example .env
   ```
   Ensure the API URL matches your running backend:
   ```env
   VITE_API_URL=http://localhost:3001
   ```

### Step 3: Run the Services

1. **Start the Backend server** (runs on port 3001 by default):
   ```bash
   cd backend
   # Starts in watch mode
   npm run dev
   ```
2. **Start the Frontend development server** (runs on port 5173 by default):
   ```bash
   cd frontend
   npm run dev
   ```
3. Open `http://localhost:5173` in your browser.

---

## Demo & Testing Guide

For quick testing, you can use the built-in demo credentials on the login screen or register an anonymous alias (guest mode).

### Testing the Concurrent Auction Lifecycle

1. **Setup Catalog**: Log in as Host A, create a room, and add at least two items to the catalog.
2. **Join Bidders**: Open an Incognito Window or separate browser profile, register a bidder alias, and join using the room code generated by Host A.
3. **Launch Auction**: Host A clicks **Start Live Auction**. Both screens will synchronize and transition into the Live Auction Dashboard.
4. **Place Bids**: Submit bids from multiple tabs simultaneously. Verify that only higher bids are accepted, and lower or concurrent slower bids are rejected atomically with real-time feedback.
5. **Item Completion**: When the timer expires or the host resolves the item, the system automatically loads the next item in the catalog.
6. **Results**: Once all items are resolved, all connected clients navigate automatically to the final results screen.

---

## API Documentation

### Authentication Endpoints

- `POST /api/auth/register` - Create a new user account.
- `POST /api/auth/login` - Authenticate and obtain JWT cookie.
- `POST /api/auth/logout` - Clear user authentication cookie.
- `GET /api/auth/me` - Get the current authenticated user context.

### Room Endpoints

- `POST /api/rooms` - Create a new auction room.
- `POST /api/rooms/:code/join` - Join an existing room with a code and alias.
- `GET /api/rooms/:code/summary` - Get details of an active room.
- `GET /api/rooms/:code/results` - Fetch final results of a completed room auction.

### Item Endpoints

- `POST /api/items` - Add a new item to a room's catalog.
- `GET /api/items/room/:roomId` - Retrieve catalog items for a room.

---

## Future Roadmap

- **Team Bidding Budgets**: Group budgets and spend caps for collaborative bidding structures.
- **Live Chat & Reactions**: Enhance bidder engagement with interactive channels on the auction page.
- **Horizontal Scaling**: Transition the WebSocket layer to a Redis-backed Socket.IO adapter for multi-instance load balancing.
- **Bidding Pause/Resume Controls**: Empower hosts to pause and resume active countdowns.
- **Spectator Support**: Allow read-only viewer roles to follow live auctions without participating.

---

# System Architecture

This document describes the high-level architecture, data models, real-time event mapping, and concurrency mechanisms used in the Mini Realtime Auction Room platform.

---

## Architecture Overview

The platform uses a decoupled client-server architecture with state kept authoritative on the server and persisted in MongoDB.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  subgraph Frontend [React Application]
    C["React Client (Vite)"]
    Z["Zustand Client Store"]
    C <--> Z
  end

  subgraph Backend [NodeJS Server]
    API["Express HTTP API"]
    SIO["Socket.IO Server"]
    T["In-Memory Room Timers"]
  end

  DB[("MongoDB Database")]

  C -->|"REST (Auth, Room Lifecycle)"| API
  C <-->|"Socket.IO (Live Bids, Presence)"| SIO
  API --> DB
  SIO --> DB
  T --> SIO
```

### Components

1. **React Frontend**: Built with React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Zustand. State is synced dynamically via Socket.IO, but auth/login and initialization happen via REST API calls. Zustand is used purely for lightweight client-side convenience (e.g., maintaining the session room token).
2. **Express API**: Handles user authentication (JWT-based), creating/joining rooms, retrieving room summaries, and catalog initialization.
3. **Socket.IO Server**: Manages full-duplex realtime connections, participant presence (joined/left indicators), live bid submissions, and live active item status updates.
4. **In-Memory Room Timers**: The server schedules and tracks active-item countdowns in memory. When a timer expires, the server automatically resolves the item status.
5. **MongoDB**: The single source of truth for all database collections (Rooms, Participants, AuctionItems, Bids).

---

## Real-Time Socket.IO Lifecycle

Socket connections are room-scoped. The client sends a per-room `sessionToken` during the handshake, and the server joins the socket to a room channel (`room:{code}`).

### Event Map

| Event Name | Direction | Payload | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `room:connect` | Client → Server | `RoomConnectPayload` | Re-establishes a room session, triggering a full state synchronization. |
| `room:state` | Server → Client | `RoomStatePayload` | Emitted immediately after room connection; contains active item, participants list, and current bids. |
| `participant:joined` | Server → Client | `Participant` | Sent to the room channel when a new bidder connects. |
| `participant:left` | Server → Client | `Participant` | Sent to the room channel when a bidder disconnects or closes their tab. |
| `auction:start` | Client → Server | *None* | Emitted by the host to activate the auction lifecycle. |
| `auction:started` | Server → Client | *None* | Signals all participants in the room to transition from the Lobby to the Auction board. |
| `item:activated` | Server → Client | `AuctionItem` | Broadcasts details of the current active item and the synchronized countdown `endsAt`. |
| `bid:place` | Client → Server | `{ amount: number }` | Submitted by bidders to place a bid. |
| `bid:accepted` | Server → Client | `{ item: AuctionItem, bids: Bid[] }` | Broadcasts the updated highest bid and history to all room participants. |
| `bid:rejected` | Server → Client | `{ reason: string, minimumBid: number }` | Sent privately to the sender socket when a bid fails validation. |
| `item:sell` | Client → Server | *None* | Emitted by the host to manually resolve the active item as "sold". |
| `item:unsold` | Client → Server | *None* | Emitted by the host to manually resolve the active item as "unsold". |
| `item:ended` | Server → Client | `{ item: AuctionItem, resolution: "sold" \| "unsold" }` | Signals that the active item is resolved. |
| `auction:completed` | Server → Client | *None* | Signals that all catalog items are resolved and redirect participants to the results dashboard. |

---

## Concurrency and Race Conditions

Handling highly concurrent live bids and timer-expiration states is a core requirement of a robust auction engine. The system achieves complete correctness using server-authoritative logic and atomic database updates.

### 1. Atomic Bids (`findOneAndUpdate`)
When multiple bidders submit identical or incremental bids simultaneously, standard read-then-write patterns can cause double-bidding or accepting a bid below the minimum.
To prevent this, the server processes bids using a single conditional MongoDB query:
```typescript
const updatedItem = await AuctionItem.findOneAndUpdate(
  {
    _id: itemId,
    status: "active",
    endsAt: { $gt: new Date() },
    currentBid: { $lt: amount }
  },
  {
    $set: {
      currentBid: amount,
      highestBidderId: participantId
    }
  },
  { new: true }
);
```
Only one database execution can succeed in updating the document first; any concurrent execution racing against the same or lower amount will fail to match the query filter (`currentBid: { $lt: amount }`) and will return `null`. The loser is rejected gracefully and receive a `bid:rejected` event with the updated current minimum bid.

### 2. Item Resolution Races
An active item can be resolved in three ways:
1. The countdown timer expires naturally.
2. The Host clicks "Sell" manually.
3. The Host clicks "Mark Unsold" manually.

To prevent multiple resolutions from firing, the resolution state transition is also atomic:
```typescript
const resolvedItem = await AuctionItem.findOneAndUpdate(
  {
    _id: itemId,
    status: "active"
  },
  {
    $set: {
      status: resolution,
      endsAt: new Date()
    }
  },
  { new: true }
);
```
If the timer expires at the exact millisecond the host clicks "Sell", only one update operation transitions the status from `"active"` to `"sold"` (or `"unsold"`). The subsequent request will fail to match `status: "active"` and will instantly no-op, avoiding duplicate catalog progression or data corruption.

### 3. Server Resiliency & Timer Restoration
To avoid losing countdown timers on server crashes or restarts, the system saves the absolute `endsAt` timestamp of the active item to MongoDB. 
Upon startup, the server automatically queries all active rooms and schedules in-memory timeouts matching the remaining duration:
```typescript
// On server boot:
const liveRooms = await Room.find({ status: "live" });
for (const room of liveRooms) {
  if (room.currentItemId && room.endsAt) {
    const remainingMs = room.endsAt.getTime() - Date.now();
    scheduleAuctionTimer(io, room._id.toString(), Math.max(0, remainingMs));
  }
}
```

---

## Database Schema

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                           rooms                             │
├─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ code (String, UQ)   │ status (Enum)    │ adminParticipantId │
│ name (String)       │ currentItemId    │ endsAt (Date)      │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────┘
                                   │
                                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        auctionitems                         │
├─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ roomId (FK)         │ startingBid (No) │ status (Enum)      │
│ title (String)      │ currentBid (No)  │ endsAt (Date)      │
│ description (Str)   │ highestBidderId  │                    │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────┘
                                   ▲
                                   │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                            bids                             │
├─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ roomId (FK)         │ participantId    │ amount (Number)    │
│ itemId (FK)         │ username (String)│ createdAt (Date)   │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────┘
                                   ▲
                                   │
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        participants                         │
├─────────────────────┬──────────────────┬────────────────────┤
│ roomId (FK)         │ role (Enum)      │ isConnected (Bool) │
│ username (String)   │ sessionToken (UQ)│                    │
└─────────────────────┴──────────────────┴────────────────────┘
```

- **Unique Constraints**: `participants` has a compound unique index on `{ roomId, usernameNormalized }` to enforce unique nicknames within a room while allowing nick reuse across other rooms.
- **Session Security**: The host/bidder role is assigned server-side during room creation/joining and encoded inside a cryptographically secure `sessionToken`, which must match the participant record during socket handshakes.

); } === DECISIONS === # Design Decisions & Architecture Trade-offs This document outlines key technical decisions, architectural trade-offs, and design rationales made during the development of the Mini Realtime Auction Room platform. --- ## 1. Real-time Communication Stack: Socket.IO vs. Native WebSockets **Decision:** We chose **Socket.IO** over native WebSockets (`ws`). ### Rationale - **Automatic Reconnection:** Live auctions require continuous connectivity. Socket.IO provides robust automatic reconnection out-of-the-box, ensuring users are seamlessly reconnected if they temporarily lose network coverage. - **Room-Scoped Messaging:** Socket.IO's native concept of "Rooms" maps perfectly to auction rooms. Moving a socket to a room (`socket.join("room:" + code)`) allows us to broadcast events like bids and presence updates only to relevant users without maintaining complex manual mapping structures. - **Heartbeats & Presence:** In-built ping/pong mechanism allows accurate and fast detection of socket disconnects, which drives our live connection status badges (the participant presence list). --- ## 2. Server-Authoritative Timer & Clock Sync **Decision:** The item countdown timer is owned entirely by the server; the client only renders the countdown using the absolute deadline timestamp (`endsAt`). ### Rationale - **Prevention of Cheat/Exploits:** If the countdown is client-driven, a malicious bidder could delay their local clock to submit bids after the timer should have expired. By storing `endsAt` on the server and executing the expiration on a server-owned `setTimeout`, cheating is eliminated. - **Restoration Resiliency:** Because `endsAt` is stored as an absolute UTC date in MongoDB, a server crash or database disconnection does not reset the timer duration when the backend restarts. The server simply query active rooms and schedules the timer for `endsAt - now`. - **Clock Drift Mitigation:** Bids are validated against the server's database time. Clients receive the target `endsAt` and count down locally relative to their own system clock. If a client's system clock is drifted, the backend's strict verification still prevents late bids. --- ## 3. Storage Strategy: MongoDB and Mongoose **Decision:** **MongoDB** was selected as the database, and Mongoose for Object-Document Mapping (ODM). ### Rationale - **Document Model Alignment:** Auction catalogs, participant lists, and bid histories are document-centric and map naturally to nested JSON documents. - **Atomic Operations:** MongoDB's `findOneAndUpdate` supports conditional updates. This allowed us to implement lock-free concurrent bid validation and item status transitions directly at the database layer (preventing race conditions) without introducing complex distributed lock managers like Redis. --- ## 4. Authentication Architecture: Dual-Layer Auth **Decision:** The application employs a two-tier authentication structure: 1. **Global Authentication (JWT Cookie):** Tracks global identity (`admin`, `demo`, or guest) and protects backend endpoints. 2. **Room Session Authorization (`sessionToken`):** Issued on room creation or join, and stored in the client session. It determines the role (`admin` or `participant`) in that specific room. ### Rationale - **Decoupled Roles:** A user may be logged in globally as `admin` but join another host's room as a `participant` (bidder). Decoupling room-specific roles from the global auth token allows participants to play different roles across different rooms without re-authenticating. - **Socket Handshake Security:** Socket.IO handshakes use the `sessionToken` to verify the socket's room eligibility, preventing unauthorized clients from listening to room channels. --- ## 5. Single-Process In-Memory Timers (Trade-off & Scaling) **Decision:** Active room timers are kept in memory using a simple Map of `NodeJS.Timeout` IDs keyed by Room ID. ### Trade-off - **Scaling Limit:** This design requires the WebSocket server to be single-instance. If we scale horizontally behind a load balancer, client connections would be split across instances, and the timer Map would be fragmented (e.g. Instance A would not be able to clear or modify a timer scheduled on Instance B). - **Mitigation/Path Forward:** For high-throughput scaling, we would introduce a Redis-backed Adapter for Socket.IO events and move timer management to a distributed job scheduler (such as BullMQ) backed by Redis. However, for a single-node deployment, in-memory timers are extremely lightweight, zero-dependency, and offer microsecond performance.

I've read the whole thing — backend (`src/**`), frontend (`src/**`), and the three docs. Both projects typecheck clean; frontend `npm run lint` fails on one rule. Here's everything worth fixing, ordered by what actually breaks.

---

## Tier 1 — Correctness bugs in the auction engine

**1. A stale expiry timer can end an item whose deadline a bid just extended.**
`resolutionHandler.ts:18-27` + `115-119`, `biddingHandler.ts:98-138`

Every accepted bid resets `endsAt` to a full duration and calls `scheduleAuctionTimer`, which calls `clearTimeout` on the old timer. But if that old timer's callback has *already fired* and is sitting in an `await` (two DB round trips inside `expireActiveItem`), `clearTimeout` is a no-op. The expiry then runs `findOneAndUpdate({ _id, status: "active" })` — **no `endsAt` condition** — and resolves the item anyway.

Observable result: bid lands at T+59.9s, everyone sees the timer jump back to 60s, then ~5ms later the item sells. The anti-snipe extension silently fails at exactly the moment it exists for.

*Exact fix:* pass the `endsAt` the timer was scheduled for into the callback, and add `endsAt: { $lte: new Date() }` (or an exact match on the expected deadline) to the filter on the `"expired"` path only. Manual host sell/unsold must stay unconditional.

**2. The Bid document is written before the atomic claim, then deleted if the claim loses.**
`biddingHandler.ts:87-119`

`newBid.save()` runs first; if `findOneAndUpdate` returns null you `Bid.deleteOne`. Two consequences: a concurrent `room:connect` doing `Bid.find({ itemId })` (`roomHandler.ts:59`) can read a bid that is about to be deleted, and a crash between the two lines orphans a rejected bid in the history forever.

*Exact fix:* invert the order. Do the conditional `findOneAndUpdate` first; only on success construct and save the Bid. This deletes the compensating `deleteOne` entirely and removes the phantom-read window. This is also the question an interviewer will ask about this file.

**3. `isConnected` is never reset on boot, so presence is wrong after every restart.**
`roomHandler.ts:45,116` + `index.ts:24-30`

The `participantSockets` map is in-memory; the `isConnected` flag is in Mongo. A crash or redeploy loses the map but leaves every participant flagged online permanently. `restoreAuctionTimers` rebuilds timers but nothing rebuilds presence.

*Exact fix:* in the `connectDB().then(...)` block, before restoring timers, run `Participant.updateMany({ isConnected: true }, { $set: { isConnected: false } })`.

**4. `endsAt` is stored twice and hand-synced.**
`roomModel.ts:46`, `itemModel.ts:59`

Three places write both copies (`auctionHandler.ts:58-64`, `biddingHandler.ts:98-137`, `resolutionHandler.ts:37-46`) and resolution writes neither. The client counts down off `room.endsAt` while the server validates bids against `item.endsAt`. They agree today only because every write path remembers to update both.

*Exact fix:* make the item the single authority. Drop `endsAt` off Room and have `restoreAuctionTimers` read it via `currentItemId`. If you'd rather not migrate, keep it but write both in one place — a small `setActiveDeadline(roomId, itemId, endsAt)` helper called by all three sites.

---

## Tier 2 — Security

**5. Room create/join/read endpoints have no authentication at all.**
`roomRoutes.ts:12-15`, `roomController.ts:16,35`

`optionalAuth` never blocks, and the controllers fall back to `req.body.username`. `curl -X POST /api/rooms/ABC123/join -d '{"username":"whoever"}'` works with no cookie. `GET /:code` and `/:code/results` are fully public. `DECISIONS.md` §4 claims the JWT cookie "protects backend endpoints" — it protects nothing.

*Exact fix:* add a `requireAuth` middleware next to `optionalAuth` that 401s when the cookie is missing or invalid; apply it to `POST /` and `POST /:code/join`; delete the `|| req.body.username` fallbacks so identity comes only from the token. For the two GETs, gate on `extractSessionToken` + a participant lookup, or consciously decide they're public and say so in the docs.

**6. Password hashing is too weak and compared non-constant-time.**
`authController.ts:24,93`

PBKDF2-SHA512 at **1,000 iterations** (OWASP's floor is 210,000), and `checkHash !== user.passwordHash` is a short-circuiting string compare.

*Exact fix:* raise iterations to 210,000, store the iteration count on the user document so existing hashes stay verifiable, and compare with `crypto.timingSafeEqual` over Buffers.

**7. The hardcoded `admin` / `password123` account is both a backdoor and dead weight.**
`authController.ts:71-75`

Anyone can log in as `admin` and get a JWT with `role: "admin"` — but grep the backend: that role is never read anywhere. Room authority comes entirely from the participant `role` set at room creation. So it grants nothing while looking like it grants everything.

*Exact fix:* delete the `admin` branch. Keep the `demo` branch (it's a genuine reviewer convenience), and update the README's "demo credentials" line, which currently advertises both.

**8. `demoCounter` is process-local.**
`authController.ts:17,80`

After a restart the counter resets to 0, so a fresh `demo_1` trying to join a room that already contains `demo_1` gets "Username is already taken."

*Exact fix:* replace with a short random suffix (`demo_${crypto.randomBytes(3).toString("hex")}`).

---

## Tier 3 — Client bugs

**9. "Leave Room" signs you out of the app.**
`LobbyPage.tsx:68-71`, `AuctionPage.tsx:137-140`

Both call `clearSession()`, which nulls `authUser` too (`useSessionStore.ts:34-42`). You land on the auth portal — but the JWT cookie is still set, so a refresh logs you straight back in. Inconsistent, and it forces a re-login to join a second room.

*Exact fix:* add a `clearRoomSession()` action that clears only the five room fields; use it for both Leave buttons. Keep `clearSession()` for Navbar logout.

**10. Missing-session users get the wrong error screen.**
`AuctionPage.tsx:182-240`, `LobbyPage.tsx:130-188`

With no `sessionToken`, `useSocket` returns `error: "Active session not found..."` (`useSocket.ts:147`), which trips the `socketError` branch first. The "Access Denied / Join Room" branch below it is unreachable in that case — users see "Realtime Connection Failed" and a Back-to-Home button instead of a working Join link.

*Exact fix:* move the `hasNoAccess` guard above the loading and error branches in both files.

**11. Room codes in URLs are compared case-sensitively.**
`AuctionPage.tsx:128`, `LobbyPage.tsx:55`

`sessionRoomCode !== code` — `/lobby/abc123` locks out a user with a valid session for `ABC123`.

*Exact fix:* normalize once at the top: `const code = rawCode?.toUpperCase()`.

**12. Presence flickers for everyone on the lobby → auction transition.**
`useSocket.ts:133`

The cleanup calls `disconnectSocket()` unconditionally. Navigating lobby → auction unmounts one `useSocket` and mounts another, so the server sees disconnect → `participant:left` broadcast → reconnect → `participant:joined`. Every other client watches that person blink offline. React StrictMode doubles this in dev.

*Exact fix:* don't disconnect on unmount when the next mount wants the same room+token. Simplest version: skip `disconnectSocket()` in cleanup and let `connectSocket`'s existing identity check (`socket.ts:17-28`) tear down only on an actual room/participant change; disconnect explicitly in the Leave handlers instead.

**13. Toast listeners attach to a possibly-null socket and never retry.**
`AuctionPage.tsx:77-125`

`getSocket()` returns null when `sessionToken` is absent, and the effect's only dependency is `addToast` — it never re-runs once a socket exists.

*Exact fix:* add `socketStatus` to the dependency array so the listeners re-bind on connect.

**14. Client clock skew can lock a bidder out.**
`AuctionPage.tsx:65-68,396`

The bid form renders only when `secondsRemaining > 0`, computed from the browser clock against the server's `endsAt`. A client 30s fast sees 0s and gets no input box while the server would happily accept the bid. `DECISIONS.md` §2 claims clock drift is mitigated — it's mitigated against *cheating*, not against honest skew locking someone out.

*Exact fix:* `item:activated` already sends `startedAt` (server `now`), and `useSocket.ts:23,143` already stores it as `activeItemStartedAt` — currently **dead state, read by nobody**. Compute `offset = Date.parse(startedAt) - Date.now()` on receipt and add it to `clockNow`.

**15. Nobody can bid the advertised starting price.**
`itemService.ts:61`, `biddingHandler.ts:77`

Items are created with `currentBid = startingBid`, and the minimum is `currentBid + 1`. An item listed at ₹500 must open at ₹501.

*Exact fix:* create with `currentBid: 0`, and compute the minimum as `Math.max(startingBid, currentBid + 1)` on both server and client. Verify the results page, which falls back to `startingBid` when `currentBid` is 0 — that fallback becomes load-bearing.

**16. `npm run lint` fails.**
`AuthInitializer.tsx:42` — `react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`. Fix or add a scoped disable with a one-line reason. A portfolio repo whose lint script exits non-zero is a bad first impression.

---

## Tier 4 — Data layer

**17. Missing indexes on the hot queries.** `Bid.find({ itemId }).sort({ createdAt: -1 })` (`roomHandler.ts:59`) and the `{ roomId, status: "pending" }` claim in `progressAuction` (`resolutionHandler.ts:55-59`) both scan. Add `BidSchema.index({ itemId: 1, createdAt: -1 })` and `AuctionItemSchema.index({ roomId: 1, status: 1, createdAt: 1 })`.

**18. Duplicate-username join is a read-then-write race** (`roomService.ts:78-95`). The compound unique index saves you, but the error surfaces as "A record with these details already exists" (`errorHandler.ts:24`). Catch code 11000 in `joinRoom` and rethrow the specific message.

**19. `PORT` isn't validated** (`env.ts:26`) — a garbage value yields `NaN` and Node binds a random port. Use the existing `getPositiveInteger` helper.

---

## Tier 5 — Documentation drift

This is the tier most likely to cost you in an interview, because the reviewer reads the docs first and diffs them against the code.

**20. Three of the six documented REST endpoints don't exist.** README:150-169 lists `POST /api/items`, `GET /api/items/room/:roomId`, `GET /api/rooms/:code/summary`. Actual: `POST|GET /api/rooms/:code/items`, `GET /api/rooms/:code`.

**21. The ARCHITECTURE.md event map is wrong on six of thirteen payloads.** `bid:accepted` is `{ bid, item }` not `{ item, bids[] }`; `auction:started` and `auction:completed` both carry `{ room }`, documented as *None*; `item:activated` is `{ item, startedAt, endsAt }`; `participant:joined/left` wrap in `{ participant }`; `room:connect` takes no payload. `item:added` and `error` are emitted but absent from the table.

**22. Both concurrency code snippets in ARCHITECTURE.md are stale.** The bid snippet (line 77) omits the `endsAt` extension that the real handler does; the resolution snippet (line 103) shows `$set: { endsAt: new Date() }`, which the real code doesn't write; the restore snippet (line 128) passes `remainingMs` where the real `scheduleAuctionTimer` takes a `Date`.

**23. The anti-snipe timer extension is documented nowhere.** Resetting the countdown on every bid is your most interesting design decision and it appears in neither README, ARCHITECTURE, nor DECISIONS. It deserves its own DECISIONS section — including the bounded-vs-unbounded trade-off (right now an item can be extended forever).

**24. Smaller lies:** `DECISIONS.md` §4 on JWT protecting endpoints (see #5); README:123 says `npm run dev` "starts in watch mode" — it's `npm run build && node server.js`, no watch; the `users` collection is missing from the ARCHITECTURE schema diagram; README:40 links ARCHITECTURE.md by absolute `file:///Users/arnavsingla/...` path, which is broken for every reader but you.

---

## Tier 6 — Repo hygiene

- **Dead code:** `features/lobby/RoomPage.tsx` (placeholder, unrouted), `stores/useUiStore.ts` (zero imports), `api.ts` `healthCheck`/`getRoom`/`getAuctionItems` (zero callers).
- **"Later milestones" placeholders:** `frontend/src/types/index.ts` and `backend/src/types/index.ts` both open with "will be added in later milestones." Delete or fill.
- **`.gitkeep` files** left in directories that now have real files (`frontend/src/{utils,hooks}`, `backend/src/{utils,models,services,socket/handlers,socket/middleware}`).
- **Root `.env.example`** duplicates `backend/.env.example` with no root package to consume it; **root `node_modules/`** holds a stray `@types` install with no `package.json`; **`main/preview.jpeg`** is committed but referenced nowhere.
- **`backend/dist/` has stale duplicates** from an old naming scheme (`room.handler.js` *and* `roomHandler.js`) — `tsc` never cleans. Make build `rm -rf dist && tsc`.
- **`@types/*` split inconsistently:** cookie-parser/express/jsonwebtoken are in `dependencies`, `@types/cors` is in `devDependencies` — a `npm ci --omit=dev && npm run build` fails. Pick one and be consistent.
- **`dev` script has no watch** despite `tsx` being installed and unused. `"dev": "tsx watch src/index.ts"`.

---

## Tier 7 — Tests

`auctionTest.ts` has three assertions against pure helpers. Nothing tests the concurrency the README leads with. **This is the single highest-value addition to the repo.** Add `mongodb-memory-server` and write three integration tests: (a) N concurrent bids at the same amount → exactly one accepted, N-1 rejected; (b) host sell racing timer expiry → exactly one `item:ended`; (c) bid accepted at T-1ms → item is *not* resolved by the stale timer. Test (c) fails today — it's the regression test for bug #1.

---

## Suggested execution order

Two to three files per batch, test, commit, continue:

1. Bug #1 + #2 — `resolutionHandler.ts`, `biddingHandler.ts` (the two that change auction outcomes)
2. Bug #3 + #17 — `index.ts`, `bidModel.ts`, `itemModel.ts`
3. Security #5 + #7 — `authMiddleware.ts`, `roomRoutes.ts`, `roomController.ts`
4. Security #6 + #8 — `authController.ts`, `userModel.ts`
5. Client #9–#11 — `useSessionStore.ts`, `LobbyPage.tsx`, `AuctionPage.tsx`
6. Client #12–#14 — `useSocket.ts`, `AuctionPage.tsx`
7. Tests (Tier 7)
8. Docs (Tier 5) + hygiene (Tier 6) last, once behavior is final

Before you call it done: draw the request flow for a bid end-to-end (socket handshake → auth middleware → `bid:place` → atomic claim → broadcast) and rehearse "what happens if two bids for the same amount arrive in the same millisecond" and "what breaks if you run two instances behind a load balancer" — #1 and the in-memory timer Map are where a sharp interviewer will push.

Tell me which batch to start with and I'll walk you through it.

11auction Assignment
Overview
You may choose any one of the project options below and build it end to end.
We expect you to use AI coding tools while building this assignment. The goal is not to prove that you can write every line manually. The goal is to see whether you can use AI well, make good technical decisions, build a real product, debug issues, and ship something clean, usable, and maintainable.
Your submission must include:
A GitHub repository
A hosted live link
A clear README.md
AI coding transcripts or session exports
A short explanation of your architecture, assumptions, and tradeoffs
Frontend design, responsiveness, usability, and polish will be considered during evaluation.
General Requirements
Technical Requirements
Your project must include:
Authentication or user/session identity
Persistent database storage
Clean frontend UI
Seed/demo data or a clear demo flow
Hosted deployment
Basic error handling
Loading and empty states
A clear separation between frontend, backend, database, and realtime logic (if present)
You may use any stack and services/libraries you want, but we recommend staying within the TypeScript ecosystem. Choose tools that make sense for the product.
Hosting Requirements
You must provide a working live URL.
The hosted app should have:
Demo credentials, or
A public demo mode
Code Quality Expectations
Your code should be:
Modular
Readable
Reasonably typed, if your stack supports it
Able to handle basic concurrent use
We do not expect a perfect production system, but we do expect evidence that you understand how production software is shaped.
AI Usage Requirement
You are expected to use AI coding tools such as Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, or similar tools.
Along with your submission, include:
The AI tool or tools used
The main prompts/sessions used
Transcript exports, share links, screenshots, or copied chat logs
A short note explaining where AI helped and where you made manual decisions
You may redact secrets, API keys, personal tokens, and private account details.
Do not fabricate transcripts. We are not judging you for using AI. We are judging how well you directed it.
How To Submit AI Transcripts
Provide a folder in your repo named:
ai-transcripts/
​
Inside it, include exports such as:
ai-transcripts/
  codex-session-1.md
  claude-session-1.txt
  cursor-session-1.md
  opencode-share-links.md
  ai-usage-summary.md
​
Your ai-usage-summary.md should include:
# AI Usage Summary

Tools used:
- Claude Code
- Cursor

- Initial architecture
- Realtime implementation
- UI component generation
- Debugging deployment issues

Important manual decisions:
- Chose PostgreSQL because...

- ...

Codex

Exported conversation text or Markdown, if available
Copied session transcript
Screenshots of the main session
Local session JSONL files, if available, commonly under a .codex or ~/.codex/sessions style session directory
Claude Code
Claude Code supports exporting the current conversation with /export. You can save it as a text file and include it in ai-transcripts/.
Claude's documentation also describes local JSONL transcripts under:
~/.claude/projects/<project>/<session-id>.jsonl
​
You may include the exported text file or the JSONL transcript.
Reference: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sessions
OpenCode
OpenCode supports sharing a conversation with:
/share
​
This creates a share link for the current conversation. Add the links to:
ai-transcripts/opencode-share-links.md
​
Reference: https://opencode.ai/docs
Cursor
If using Cursor, submit one of:
Exported/copied chat or composer history
A screen recording if export is not available in your setup
The minimum expectation is that we can see the major prompts, decisions, and debugging steps.
Project Options
Choose one of the following.
Option 1: AI Memory Journal
Problem Statement
People forget many small but meaningful details from their daily lives. Photos capture some memories, but they often miss the context: who was there, what happened, how the person felt, what decisions were made, and why the day mattered.
Build an AI-powered personal memory journal.
The user should be able to record (by voice) or write a short daily entry. Ideally, this can be a 3-5 minute voice conversation with the AI at the end of the day. The AI should turn that input into a clean, beautiful journal entry.
The app should extract important memories from the conversation and store them in a way that can be searched later.
For example, years later the user should be able to ask:
"When did I first meet Rohan?"
"What did I do on my birthday last year?"
"When did I visit Goa?"
"What was I worried about during my first job interview?"
The AI should answer using stored journal memories, ideally with references to the relevant journal entries.
Core Features
Your app should include:
Daily journal entry creation
Text input, voice input, or both
AI-generated journal summary
Extracted people, places, events, moods, and decisions
Search or chat over past memories
A timeline/calendar view of entries
A visually pleasant journal reading experience
Optional Features
You may add:
AI-generated images or visual cards for journal entries
Mood trends over time
Memory graph of people, places, and events
Private/public entry settings
Tags
Voice transcription
Export to PDF or Markdown
The goal is to build a beautiful, AI-assisted personal memory journal app.
Assumptions To State
In your README, clearly mention assumptions, if any.
Option 2: Mini AI Design Mode
Problem Statement
Many developers can build functional screens, but struggle to make them look polished. Build a small AI design mode tool that helps improve UI screens.
The user should be able to open or upload a web page, and ask the AI to improve it. The best example would be agentation.dev (how we can select components), and how Cursor built it's design mode. The goal is to be able to easily point at components and ask the AI to improve them.
For example:
"Improve the spacing and hierarchy."
"Make this empty state look better."
"Suggest a better mobile layout."
"Make this pricing card more premium."
The app should give useful design suggestions and, where possible, produce updated code, CSS, or a visual preview.
This does not need to be a full Cursor clone. Keep the scope focused and polished.
Core Features
Your app should include:
A page/component/screenshot review interface
AI-generated design feedback
Before/after view
Ability to accept or reject suggestions
Basic code or CSS output
A clean, visual interface
Assumptions To State
In your README, clearly mention assumptions, if any.
Option 3: Mini Realtime Auction Room
Problem Statement
Build a realtime auction room similar in spirit to the auction room experience in iplauction.
This does not need to be sports-specific, but the interaction should feel like a real live auction room: users join a room, the admin starts the auction, one item/player is presented at a time, people bid live, a timer runs, and the item is sold or marked unsold.
The product should feel live, competitive, and reliable. The auction logic should be of the main priority.
Example domains:
Cricket/football fantasy auction
Collectibles auction
Art auction
Sneakers auction
Domain name auction
Office charity auction
The important part is the room experience.
Core Features
Your app should include:
Create auction room
Join room by code/link
Admin and participant roles
Item/player list
Start auction
Current item/player display
Countdown timer
Realtime bidding
Bid history
Sold/unsold outcome
Final results page
Basic room state persistence
Expected Auction Flow
A reasonable flow would be:
LOBBY -> AUCTION -> COMPLETED
​
During the auction:
Only one item/player is active at a time
Users can place bids while the timer is active
Highest bid is visible to everyone
Bid history updates live
Timer expiry resolves the item
Admin can pause/end if needed
Results show who won what and for how much
Optional Features
You may add:
Skip/withdraw voting
Team/squad budgets
Maximum items per user
Role/category caps
Chat/reactions
Public/private rooms
Auction pause/resume
Presence indicators
Spectator mode
Realtime Requirement
Realtime is central to this project.
At minimum:
Bids must update live
Current item/player must update live
Timer state must stay reasonably synced
Results should update without manual refresh
Assumptions To State
In your README, clearly mention assumptions, if any.
Option 4: Watch Together Platform
Problem Statement
Watching videos with friends remotely is harder than it should be. Build a watch-party platform where one user creates a room, adds a YouTube link or video link, invites friends, and everyone watches together.
The video should stay synchronized across users. If one user pauses, resumes, or seeks, the room should update for everyone.
The app should also include realtime chat so people can react while watching.
Core Features
Your app should include:
Create watch room
Join room by link/code
Add YouTube/video URL
Shared video player
Realtime play/pause/seek sync
Realtime chat
Room participants list
Late joiner sync
Basic room persistence
Optional Features
You may add:

Watch queue
User presence
Room history
Private/public rooms
Voice notes
Polls
Start-at-same-time countdown
Mobile-friendly viewing mode
Realtime Requirement
Realtime is central to this project.

Assumptions To State
In your README, clearly mention assumptions, if any.
Evaluation Criteria
1. Product Completeness
Does the app solve the stated problem?

2. Realtime Correctness

6. AI Usage Quality

7. Communication

Final Submission Checklist

## What I actually verified, live, just now

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| `auction-assignment.vercel.app` | 200, 0.37s |
| `live-auction-fhb9.onrender.com/health` | 200, 0.34s (service awake) |

| Host `item:sell` → `auction:completed` | both fired |
| Register a brand-new user | 201, then login 200 |

Atlas is connected. Render is healthy. Cross-site cookies work. The atomic bid rejection works. There is nothing to restore.

**Do not create a new Atlas cluster tonight.** Repointing `MONGODB_URI` triggers a Render redeploy, and the code currently deployed calls `process.exit(1)` if the DB connection fails on boot (`connectDB`, committed version). One typo in a new connection string and you have a genuinely dead service hours before the call. You'd be introducing the exact outage you think you're fixing.

## Why you thought it was down

Render's free tier spins the service down after ~15 minutes idle; the wake takes 50-60s. Your `AuthInitializer` gives up at exactly 60s (`COLD_START_TIMEOUT_MS`, `api.ts:12`) and renders "Can't reach the server." You almost certainly opened a cold instance and hit that ceiling. It is not a bug in your code — but **it will happen to your interviewer**, which makes it the highest-priority item on this list.

## Two real problems I did find

**1. Production is writing to a database literally named `test`.** Your cluster `cluster0.kputqg8` contains:

```
test           <- your live auction data (rooms, participants, bids)
auction        <- 0 docs, stray collection (what your LOCAL .env points at)
sample_mflix   <- Atlas sample data
trello         <- a different project of yours
```

Render's `MONGODB_URI` has no database name in the path, so Mongoose defaulted to `test`. Your local `.env` says `/auction`, which is why local and prod have never shared data. If you screen-share Compass tomorrow, that's the first thing he'll see.

**2. Prod data before my probes: 1 room ("Cricket", stuck in `lobby` since Jul 28), 1 participant, 0 items, 0 bids, 0 users.** No seed data, and registration had never once been exercised in production until I tested it a minute ago. The assignment explicitly requires "Seed/demo data or a clear demo flow."

## What I'd do with the hours you have left

It's ~1:40am your time and the interview is today. Ruthless triage — **do not start the 26-item bug list**, it will cost you sleep and gain you nothing he'll see.

1. **Keep the backend warm.** UptimeRobot or cron-job.org, free, hit `/health` every 10 minutes. Five minutes of work, removes the single most likely demo failure. Also hit the URL yourself 5 minutes before the call.
2. **Commit and push the resilience work you already wrote but never pushed** (`requireDatabase.ts` is untracked; `index.ts`, `db.ts`, `app.ts`, `healthController.ts`, `AuthInitializer.tsx`, `api.ts` are modified). It binds the port before connecting to Mongo and serves 503s instead of exiting. This is a genuine improvement *and* a strong thing to talk about. Push it first, verify the deploy, and only then consider step 3.
3. **Optionally** move prod off the `test` database — one env var change on Render, but only *after* step 2 is live so a bad URI degrades instead of killing the service. Your call whether it's worth the risk; the data loss is one abandoned room.
4. **Seed a demo room** with 3-4 items so you're not typing a catalog live while he watches.
5. **Fix the README's missing live link.** The current README has no Live Demo URL at all — it was in an older commit and got dropped in the restructure. The submission checklist requires it.

Everything else from my audit is post-interview work, except as *talking points* — knowing the stale-timer race exists and being able to describe it is worth more to you tomorrow than fixing it tonight.

Two things I need from you:

**What exactly did you see** when you concluded it was down — the "Can't reach the server" screen, a Render dashboard error, a blank page? If there's a failure mode I haven't reproduced I want to chase it before we move on.

## Yes — three things need to change before you commit

All three sit *inside* the files you're about to push, so fixing them after would mean immediately amending.

**1. The frontend lint is red, in the exact file you're committing.** `npm run lint` fails on `AuthInitializer.tsx:42` (`react-hooks/set-state-in-effect`). Committing a failing lint script into a portfolio repo is worse than the bug.

**2. The resilience feature only covers half the app.** `requireDatabase` guards `/api`, but `socketAuthMiddleware` has no equivalent check. During a database outage the HTTP side returns a clean 503 while socket clients get "Authentication failed: Internal server error" — because `Participant.findOne` sits in Mongoose's buffer for 5s and then throws. Same outage, two contradictory stories. It needs an `isDatabaseConnected()` check at the top of the socket middleware. This is also the thing an interviewer would spot immediately if you present the feature as "the app degrades gracefully."

**3. `backend/src/types/index.ts` still declares `HealthResponse = { status, timestamp }`**, which your new health payload no longer matches. Stale type, unused, contradicts the code in the same commit.

I verified the rest of the diff is safe to deploy: `tsc --noEmit` passes on both projects, `/health` still returns 200 so Render's check won't flap, `requireDatabase` is a no-op while the DB is connected, and nothing reads the old health shape (`healthCheck()` in `api.ts` has no callers — it's on the dead-code list).

## Commit plan

Two commits. I've matched your repo's existing convention (`feat(auction):`, `fix(realtime):` from your recent history) rather than the casual phrasing in your example — say the word if you'd rather have the casual style and I'll rewrite them.

**Commit 1 — backend (6 files, +2 from task #1)**

```bash
git add backend/src/config/db.ts \
        backend/src/middleware/requireDatabase.ts \
        backend/src/app.ts \
        backend/src/controllers/healthController.ts \
        backend/src/index.ts \
        backend/src/socket/index.ts \
        backend/src/socket/middleware/auth.ts \
        backend/src/types/index.ts

git commit -m "fix(backend): keep serving when MongoDB is unreachable

Startup used to await the Mongo connection and exit(1) on failure, so a
database problem took the whole service down instead of degrading it. The
HTTP port now binds first and the connection retries in the background with
exponential backoff. Requests to /api return 503 while the database is down,
the socket handshake reports the same condition instead of an auth error,
and /health reports readiness separately so the platform does not restart a
process that is alive but not ready. Auction timers are restored once the
connection is actually established, and SIGTERM/SIGINT now shut down cleanly."
```

**Commit 2 — frontend (2 files)**

```bash
git add frontend/src/services/api.ts frontend/src/app/AuthInitializer.tsx

git commit -m "feat(frontend): show a recoverable state when the API is unavailable

An unreachable backend was indistinguishable from a signed-out user, so the
app rendered normally and every request failed with no explanation. checkAuth
now raises ApiUnavailableError on network failure, timeout or 5xx, and the
initialiser renders a dedicated unavailable state with a retry button. Cold
starts on the free tier get a 60s allowance and an explanatory notice after
four seconds."
```

**Then push:**

```bash
git push origin main
```

Don't run these yet — tasks 1's three fixes have to land first, and two of them add files to commit 1's list (`socket/middleware/auth.ts`, `types/index.ts`).

Writing docs before those land means rewriting twice.

content.text:
Task 1 in progress. Confirmed `HealthResponse` has **zero importers** anywhere in `src/` — it's fully dead.

Learn Mode, step 2. Three concepts, no code. The middle one is the only substantial one.

---

## Concept 1: Mongoose buffering, and why your two entry points tell different stories

**Intuition:** you built a doorman for the front door and forgot the side door.

**What happens internally.** When you call `Participant.findOne(...)` while `mongoose.connection.readyState !== 1`, Mongoose does *not* throw and does *not* touch the network. It pushes the operation into a per-model buffer queue and hands you a pending promise. The queue drains if the connection opens. `bufferTimeoutMS` — which you explicitly set to 5000 in `db.ts` — is the deadline: if the connection hasn't opened by then, the queued operation rejects with `Operation "participants.findOne()" buffering timed out after 5000ms`.

That buffering is precisely why a dead database *feels like a hang* rather than an error, which is what the comment you wrote in `db.ts` is reacting to.

Now trace both paths during an outage:

- **Express:** request → cors → json → cookieParser → `requireDatabase` reads `readyState`, short-circuits → `AppError(503)` → `errorHandler` → JSON. No model call ever happens. Fast and honest.
- **Socket.IO:** handshake → `io.use(socketAuthMiddleware)` → `Participant.findOne({sessionToken})` → buffers → 5s → rejects → your `catch` → `next(new Error("Authentication failed: Internal server error."))`.

The client gets `connect_error`; `useSocket`'s `handleConnectError` puts that string into `error`; both LobbyPage and AuctionPage render it under **"Realtime Connection Failed"**. So during a database outage your app tells the user their *authentication* failed. And because `socket.ts` sets `reconnectionAttempts: 5, reconnectionDelay: 1000`, the client burns five rounds of 5-second buffer timeouts — roughly half a minute of spinner — before settling on the wrong message.

**Architecture.** Readiness is a property of the *process*, not of a protocol. This process has two front doors: the Express middleware chain and the Socket.IO middleware chain. A readiness gate belongs at the head of each — the earliest point where you can answer "can I serve anything at all?" without touching a model. You built the primitive (`isDatabaseConnected()`), exported it, and wired it into one of the two.

**Edge case worth deciding deliberately:** the handshake guard only protects *new* connections. A socket already connected when the DB drops will send `bid:place`, buffer, time out, and hit the existing catch — which emits `bid:rejected` with "Internal server error placing bid." Technically true, unhelpfully vague. My read: guard the handshake now, leave the in-flight case, but know it's there so you can answer for it rather than be surprised by it.

**Production concern:** this isn't only cosmetic. Five retries × five seconds × every reconnecting client means thousands of queued operations holding promises and queue slots during an outage. Failing at the door is load shedding, not just better copy.

**The interview question this invites:** "You added a readiness check to your REST layer — what happens to a WebSocket client during that same outage?"

---

## Concept 2: why React's lint rule objects to your effect

**Intuition:** the effect is telling React "I know you just finished rendering — throw it away and go again."

**Internally.** React commits a render, runs layout effects, paints, then runs passive effects (`useEffect`). A passive effect that synchronously calls `setState` forces another render pass before the user sees a stable frame. React 19's compiler-era lint flags this because it's almost always one of two mistakes: state that should have been *derived during render*, or an effect that should *subscribe* rather than *push*.

**In your specific case**, look at what `initialise` does before its first `await`: `setStatus("loading")` and `setIsSlow(false)`. Now ask what those two values already are on mount — `useState<InitStatus>("loading")` and `useState(false)`. They are already exactly that. **On the mount path those two calls are no-ops** that trip the rule for zero benefit.

They exist for the *retry* path: when "Try again" calls `initialise()` from the `unavailable` state, resetting to `loading` is genuinely necessary.

So the fix isn't restructuring the component — it's recognising the reset belongs to the retry, not the mount. Two shapes achieve that, and either kills the warning *without* a disable comment. That matters: a suppression comment sitting in one of the first files an interviewer opens invites "why did you silence this?"

**The trap:** `initialise` is in the effect's dependency array via `useCallback`. Whatever you change must keep its identity stable, or the effect re-fires every render and you get an infinite auth-check loop against production. Be deliberate here.

---

## Concept 3: the stale type

`HealthResponse` declares two fields; the controller now returns five. Nothing imports it, so nothing type-checks the mirror against the original — it drifted silently and will again. A type that *duplicates* a value instead of *deriving* from it is a lie with a delay fuse. Since the file also carries the "will be added in later milestones" placeholder, deleting it outright folds cleanly into task 20.

---

**Your turn — step 3.** Explain back to me, in your own words:

1. Why does a socket client get "Authentication failed" instead of a 503 during a database outage, and where exactly does the fix belong?
2. Why are the two `setState` calls at the top of `initialise` harmless on mount but necessary on retry?

Once you've done that I'll hand you the code for all three and you type it, then we run lint and typecheck and move to the commits.

content.description: Blocking issues in the current working diff: (1) frontend `npm run lint` fails on react-hooks/set-state-in-effect at AuthInitializer.tsx:42; (2) socketAuthMiddleware has no DB-connected guard, so during an outage sockets report "Authentication failed" instead of a clear unavailable error — the HTTP half of this feature is guarded but the realtime half is not; (3) backend/src/types/index.ts still declares HealthResponse = {status,timestamp}, which no longer matches the new health payload.

content.subject: Commit and push the backend database-resilience work
content.description: Six files: config/db.ts, middleware/requireDatabase.ts (new), app.ts, controllers/healthController.ts, index.ts, socket/index.ts. Binds the HTTP port before connecting to Mongo, retries with backoff instead of process.exit(1), serves 503 from /api during an outage, reports readiness on /health, restores auction timers once connected, adds SIGTERM/SIGINT shutdown.

content.subject: Commit and push the frontend server-unavailable state
content.description: Two files: services/api.ts (ApiUnavailableError, 60s cold-start timeout, 5xx detection) and app/AuthInitializer.tsx (loading / unavailable / ready states, slow-start notice, retry button).

content.subject: Verify the Render deploy after pushing
content.description: After the push, confirm /health returns the new payload shape with ready/database/uptimeSeconds, and re-run the end-to-end auction probe (login, create room, add item, join, socket bid accept/reject, sell, complete) against production.

content.subject: Fix the stale expiry timer that can end an item a bid just extended
content.description: resolutionHandler.ts:18-27 and 115-119. Every accepted bid resets endsAt and calls scheduleAuctionTimer, which clearTimeout's the old timer — but if that timer already fired and is awaiting DB calls, clearTimeout is a no-op, and the expiry filter {_id, status:"active"} has no endsAt condition, so it resolves the item anyway. Fix: pass the scheduled endsAt into the callback and add endsAt: {$lte: now} to the expired path only. Highest-value correctness bug in the repo and the best interview talking point.
content.activeForm: Fixing the stale expiry timer race

content.subject: Write the Bid document after the atomic claim, not before
content.description: biddingHandler.ts:87-119 saves the Bid, then deletes it if findOneAndUpdate loses. A concurrent room:connect can read a bid that is about to vanish, and a crash between the two lines orphans a rejected bid forever. Invert the order so the conditional update runs first and the Bid is only written on success; the compensating deleteOne disappears.
content.activeForm: Reordering bid write after atomic claim

content.subject: Reset participant isConnected flags on server boot
content.description: Presence lives in an in-memory Map but isConnected lives in Mongo. Any restart loses the Map and leaves every participant flagged online permanently. Add Participant.updateMany({isConnected:true},{$set:{isConnected:false}}) in index.ts before restoreAuctionTimers.

content.subject: Require authentication on the room create and join endpoints
content.description: roomRoutes.ts uses optionalAuth, which never blocks, and the controllers fall back to req.body.username — so an unauthenticated curl can create or join any room as any name. DECISIONS.md section 4 claims the JWT cookie "protects backend endpoints"; it protects nothing. Add a requireAuth middleware, apply it to POST / and POST /:code/join, and delete the body fallbacks. Decide explicitly whether GET /:code and /:code/results stay public and document the answer.

content.subject: Harden the auth controller: hashing, comparison, demo accounts
content.description: authController.ts: PBKDF2-SHA512 runs at 1,000 iterations (OWASP floor is 210,000); the hash comparison uses !== on hex strings instead of crypto.timingSafeEqual; the hardcoded admin/password123 branch mints a JWT with role "admin" that no server code ever reads; demoCounter is process-local so demo_1 collides after a restart. Raise iterations and store the count per user for verifiability, use timingSafeEqual, drop the admin branch, and give demo users a random suffix.

content.subject: Fix session and routing bugs on the lobby and auction pages
content.description: Three related client bugs: (1) "Leave Room" calls clearSession(), which also nulls authUser, silently signing the user out while the JWT cookie stays set — add a clearRoomSession() that clears only room fields; (2) the hasNoAccess guard sits below the socketError guard, so a user with no session sees "Realtime Connection Failed" instead of the Join Room screen — move it above; (3) sessionRoomCode !== code compares case-sensitively, so /lobby/abc123 locks out a valid ABC123 session — normalise the param.
content.activeForm: Fixing lobby and auction session bugs

content.subject: Fix socket lifecycle, toast listeners, and client clock skew
content.description: (1) useSocket's cleanup calls disconnectSocket() unconditionally, so navigating lobby to auction makes every other client watch that participant blink offline then online; (2) AuctionPage's toast effect depends only on addToast and binds to a possibly-null getSocket(), so listeners never attach if the socket was not ready; (3) the bid form renders only when secondsRemaining > 0, computed from the browser clock, so a fast client clock hides the input even though the server would accept the bid — useSocket already stores activeItemStartedAt (server time) and nothing reads it; use it to compute an offset.
content.activeForm: Fixing socket lifecycle and clock skew

content.subject: Let bidders bid the advertised starting price
content.description: Items are created with currentBid = startingBid and the minimum is currentBid + 1, so an item listed at 500 cannot be opened at 500. Create with currentBid: 0 and compute the minimum as max(startingBid, currentBid + 1) on both server and client. Check the results page, whose startingBid fallback becomes load-bearing.

content.subject: Add the missing database indexes and clean up the join race message
content.description: Bid.find({itemId}).sort({createdAt:-1}) and the {roomId, status:"pending"} claim in progressAuction both scan. Add BidSchema.index({itemId:1, createdAt:-1}) and AuctionItemSchema.index({roomId:1, status:1, createdAt:1}). Also catch duplicate-key 11000 in joinRoom so a concurrent same-name join returns "Username is already taken in this room" instead of the generic "A record with these details already exists". Validate PORT with the existing getPositiveInteger helper.
content.activeForm: Adding indexes and fixing join errors

content.subject: Write integration tests for the concurrency the README advertises
content.description: auctionTest.ts has three assertions against pure helpers and nothing covers the atomic logic the project leads with. Add mongodb-memory-server and three tests: N concurrent equal bids yield exactly one acceptance; host sell racing timer expiry yields exactly one item:ended; a bid accepted milliseconds before expiry is not resolved by the stale timer. The third fails today and is the regression test for task #5.

content.subject: Rewrite the README against what the code actually does
content.description: The live demo URL is missing entirely (it existed in commit 8075592 and was dropped in the restructure) while the assignment checklist requires it. Three of six documented REST endpoints do not exist: POST /api/items, GET /api/items/room/:roomId and GET /api/rooms/:code/summary, versus the real POST|GET /api/rooms/:code/items and GET /api/rooms/:code. content.description: Six of thirteen documented payloads are wrong: bid:accepted is {bid,item} not {item,bids[]}; auction:started and auction:completed both carry {room} but are documented as None; item:activated is {item,startedAt,endsAt}; participant:joined and participant:left wrap in {participant}; room:connect takes no payload. item:added and error are emitted but missing from the table.
